content: The quality of evidence supporting the recommendation for psychological interventions for bereaved adults is very low. However, it is advised to follow general principles of care as outlined in the WHO (2010) mhGAP Intervention Guide. These principles emphasize effective communication, mobilizing and providing social support, and addressing overall well-being. Additionally, culturally appropriate mourning practices should be encouraged. For bereaved children and adolescents without a mental disorder, benzodiazepines should not be offered. This recommendation is strong despite the very low quality of evidence. Instead, general principles of care, as described in the WHO (2010) mhGAP Intervention Guide, should be applied. These include communication, social support, and attention to overall well-being, along with psychological first aid principles. Participation in culturally appropriate mourning should also be encouraged. In cases where a child has lost a primary caregiver, issues of protection and continued supportive caregiving, including socio-emotional support, must be addressed. The WHO plans to disseminate, adapt, and implement these recommendations through the development of an mhGAP clinical module for managing stress-related disorders and problems in adults, adolescents, and children. This module will be distributed widely via WHO regional and country offices, collaborating centers, professional organizations, and partner agencies. It will also be promoted as a WHO-UNHCR tool for humanitarian work. Evidence profiles will be uploaded to the WHO mhGAP Evidence Resource Centre, and an article will be submitted to a public health journal to share the guidelines and their development process. Adaptation for field use will involve creating suitable training materials in consultation with stakeholders and ensuring interventions are culturally acceptable and compatible with local health systems. WHO is also developing a monitoring and evaluation tool to assess the implementation of the mhGAP Intervention Guide and its stress-related module. Additionally, WHO mhGAP partners are creating their own tools to evaluate implementation. Rigorous research is needed to address gaps in evidence, particularly for scoping questions with low or very low-quality evidence. The guidelines and evidence base will be reviewed within five years. For adults with acute traumatic stress symptoms within the first month after a potentially traumatic event, early psychological interventions, such as trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), have shown evidence of reducing symptom severity. These interventions may include problem-solving counseling, relaxation techniques, psychoeducation, and CBT applied early after the event. However, the quality of evidence is limited, and further research is needed to strengthen the evidence base.
